title: Starting point check
description: 12 quick questions to see what you already know. There is no pass or fail; this helps RupeeRise pick your first activities.

questions.prompt: Sana has ₹500 left this week. Which expense is a NEED?

options.text: Bus fare to reach her exam centre
options.explanation: Reaching an exam is essential; skipping it has serious consequences.

options.text: A new phone cover her friends recommended
options.explanation: Nice to have, but her phone works without it.

options.text: A movie ticket for the weekend
options.explanation: Entertainment is a want, even when it feels important.

options.text: All of these are equally important
options.explanation: Budgeting means ranking expenses. Needs come first.

questions.prompt: Ravi gets ₹3,000 a month. His needs cost ₹2,200. What is the best plan for the remaining ₹800?

options.text: Spend it all on wants since needs are covered
options.explanation: Spending everything leaves nothing for goals or surprises.

options.text: Set aside some savings first, then use the rest for wants
options.explanation: Paying yourself first builds savings while still allowing some wants.

options.text: Keep it in his pocket and decide later
options.explanation: Unplanned money usually gets spent without noticing.

options.text: Lend it to friends so it is safe
options.explanation: Lending is not saving; it may not come back when you need it.

questions.prompt: You want to buy a ₹1,800 bicycle helmet in 3 months. How much should you save each month?

options.explanation: ₹300 × 3 = ₹900, only half the goal.
₹1,800 ÷ 3 months = ₹600 per month.

options.text: Whatever is left at month end
options.explanation: Without a target, you may reach month 3 with too little.

options.text: ₹1,800 in the last month
options.explanation: Saving everything at the end is risky and stressful.

questions.prompt: Which habit helps you save most reliably?

options.text: Saving whatever is left at the end of the month
options.explanation: Usually nothing is left. Spending expands to fill what you have.

options.text: Putting a fixed amount aside as soon as you receive money
options.explanation: Save first, spend the rest: the amount is protected before temptation.

options.text: Saving only when you get extra gift money
options.explanation: Occasional saving is good, but a regular habit grows faster.

options.text: Saving is only for people with high incomes
options.explanation: Small regular amounts add up for everyone.

questions.prompt: Why keep an emergency fund separate from your goal savings?

options.text: So surprises don't wipe out your goal or force you to borrow
options.explanation: A separate cushion protects both your goal and you from debt.

options.text: It earns much higher interest
options.explanation: Emergency money is about safety and access, not high returns.

options.text: Emergencies rarely happen, so it isn't needed
options.explanation: Repairs, illness and fees happen to almost everyone.

options.text: So you can spend it on sales and offers
options.explanation: A sale is not an emergency.

questions.prompt: ₹1,000 earns 10% interest a year. With COMPOUND interest, what happens in year 2?

options.text: You earn ₹100 again, same as year 1
options.explanation: That's simple interest. Compound interest also pays on last year's ₹100.

options.text: You earn ₹110, because interest is paid on ₹1,100
options.explanation: Compound interest: 10% of ₹1,100 = ₹110.

options.text: You earn ₹200, double the first year
options.explanation: Compounding grows steadily, not by doubling each year.

options.text: You earn nothing until the deposit ends
options.explanation: Interest accrues each period.

questions.prompt: A message promises '30% guaranteed returns every month, zero risk'. What is the most accurate thought?

options.text: Great deal; guaranteed means safe
options.explanation: Higher potential return always comes with higher risk. 'Guaranteed high returns' is a red flag.

options.text: High returns always come with risk; this is almost certainly a fraud
options.explanation: No genuine investment offers high, guaranteed, risk-free returns.

options.text: Invest a little to test it
options.explanation: Scams often pay small early returns to pull in bigger amounts.

options.text: Returns and risk are unrelated
options.explanation: They are closely linked.

questions.prompt: Which option is the most diversified?

options.text: All money in one well-known company
options.explanation: Even famous companies can fall sharply.

options.text: Money spread across a basket of many companies plus a deposit
options.explanation: Different holdings don't all fall together, which limits damage.

options.text: Three companies in the same industry
options.explanation: One industry problem hits all three at once.

options.text: Moving all money to whichever company rose most last month
options.explanation: That concentrates risk and chases the past.

questions.prompt: Your college fees are due in 10 months. Where should that money be kept?

options.text: Somewhere steady, like a deposit, because you need it soon
options.explanation: Short horizon = no time to recover from a fall.

options.text: In one fast-growing company to earn more
options.explanation: A fall right before the due date could leave you short.

options.text: In a crypto coin a friend recommended
options.explanation: Very volatile and unsuitable for money needed soon.

options.text: It doesn't matter where
options.explanation: When you need money changes how much risk you can take.

questions.prompt: A caller says he is from your bank and needs the OTP you just received to 'stop a fraud'. What do you do?

options.text: Share it quickly to protect your account
options.explanation: Banks never ask for OTPs. The caller is the fraud.

options.text: Hang up and call the number on your card or official app
options.explanation: Verify through a channel you already trust.

options.text: Share only the first three digits
options.explanation: Any part of an OTP helps fraudsters.

options.text: Ask for his employee ID, then share it
options.explanation: Fake IDs are easy to make up. Never share.

questions.prompt: An SMS says: 'Your account is blocked. Update KYC at http://deccanbank-verify.xyz'. What is the biggest warning sign?

options.text: It mentions KYC
options.explanation: KYC itself is real; the problem is how it's asked.

options.text: The urgent threat plus a look-alike web address
options.explanation: Panic + an unofficial link is a classic phishing pattern.

options.text: It came by SMS
options.explanation: Banks do send genuine SMS alerts; the content matters.

options.text: Nothing; banks often send links like this
options.explanation: Banks ask you to use their official app or branch, not random links.

questions.prompt: A job ad offers ₹3,000/day for liking videos but asks for a ₹499 registration fee. This is:

options.text: A good opportunity worth ₹499
options.explanation: Real employers pay you; they don't charge to hire you.

options.text: A scam: unrealistic pay plus an upfront fee
options.explanation: Two strong red flags together.

options.text: Safe if many people have joined
options.explanation: Scammers use fake reviews and group members.

options.text: Fine if the fee is small
options.explanation: Small fees are how these scams start.

title: Plan & Budget quiz
description: Five scenario questions on needs, wants, budgets and goals.

questions.prompt: Arjun's phone data is used for college notes and stall orders. His friend says it's a 'want'. Who is right?

options.text: Arjun: basic data is a need here because study and work depend on it
options.explanation: Context decides. A basic plan is a need; an expensive unlimited plan might be part want.

options.text: The friend: phones are always wants
options.explanation: The same item can be a need or want depending on how it's used.

options.text: Neither; everything is a need
options.explanation: Treating everything as a need makes budgeting impossible.

options.text: It depends on the phone brand
options.explanation: The use matters, not the brand.

questions.prompt: Lakshmi's planned spending adds up to ₹5,300 but her stipend is ₹5,000. What should she do first?

options.text: Borrow ₹300 from a friend every month
options.explanation: Regular borrowing to fill a gap builds debt.

options.text: Reduce wants until spending fits within ₹5,000
options.explanation: A budget must balance. Cut wants before needs.

options.text: Cut her mess food budget
options.explanation: Cutting essential food harms health and studies.

options.text: Ignore it; the extra ₹300 will work out
options.explanation: Overspending doesn't disappear; it shows up as shortages.

questions.prompt: Which goal is the most useful for planning?

options.text: 'I want to save more money'
options.explanation: No amount or deadline, so you can't track it.

options.text: 'Save ₹2,400 for a course by March, ₹800 a month'
options.explanation: Specific amount, deadline and monthly target.

options.text: 'Become rich someday'
options.explanation: Too vague to act on.

options.text: 'Save whenever I feel like it'
options.explanation: Feelings change; plans help.

questions.prompt: An unexpected ₹400 expense appears. Meera has ₹350 in wants and ₹400 in goal savings. What protects her goal best?

options.text: Take all ₹400 from goal savings
options.explanation: That fully sets back the goal when wants could absorb most of it.

options.text: Cut wants by ₹350 and use ₹50 from savings
options.explanation: Flexible spending absorbs the shock first, protecting most of the goal.

options.text: Borrow ₹400
options.explanation: Borrowing is a last resort when other options exist.

options.text: Skip a need like her bus pass
options.explanation: Skipping needs creates new problems.

questions.prompt: Imran's old sneakers still work but friends are buying new ones. His emergency fund is behind schedule. What's the wisest choice?

options.text: Buy them; he works hard and deserves it
options.explanation: Rewards are fine, but not ahead of a safety net he's behind on.

options.text: Delay the sneakers until the emergency fund is on track
options.explanation: Delaying a want protects his income if the bike breaks down.

options.text: Buy them on EMI so it feels cheaper
options.explanation: EMIs spread cost but add commitments and sometimes interest.

options.text: Stop saving for 2 months to afford them
options.explanation: Pausing saving for a want weakens his safety net.

title: Save & Manage quiz
description: Five questions on saving habits, emergency funds and interest.

questions.prompt: Lakshmi receives her stipend on the 1st. When is the best time to move ₹500 to savings?

options.text: On the 1st, right when it arrives
options.explanation: Save first so the money is protected from everyday spending.

options.text: On the 30th, if anything is left
options.explanation: By month-end the money is usually gone.

options.text: Only in months with no expenses
options.explanation: Such months never come.

options.text: After she buys everything she wants
options.explanation: Wants can expand to use everything.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a genuine use of an emergency fund?

options.text: A big festival sale on headphones
options.explanation: A sale is a want dressed up as urgency.

options.text: Medicines when you fall ill
options.explanation: Unexpected, necessary and urgent: exactly what the fund is for.

options.text: A weekend trip with friends
options.explanation: Planned fun should come from the wants budget.

options.text: Upgrading to a newer phone
options.explanation: An upgrade isn't an emergency.

questions.prompt: Two deposits pay 6% a year for 5 years. One uses simple interest, the other compound. Which ends with more?

options.text: Simple interest
options.explanation: Simple interest never earns on previous interest.

options.text: Compound interest
options.explanation: Interest earning interest grows the balance faster each year.

options.text: Both end the same
options.explanation: They match only in the first period.

options.text: Impossible to tell
options.explanation: With the same rate and time, compound always wins.

questions.prompt: Imran spends about ₹7,000 a month on essentials. A common guideline is an emergency fund covering a few months of essentials. What's a sensible first target?

options.explanation: Barely covers a small repair.

options.text: Around ₹7,000 to ₹14,000 (one to two months), building over time
options.explanation: A realistic starting cushion he can grow.

options.text: ₹2,00,000 before spending on anything
options.explanation: Unrealistic targets get abandoned.

options.text: Nothing; he can borrow if needed
options.explanation: Relying on borrowing is risky and costly.

questions.prompt: Saving ₹50 a day sounds small. Roughly how much is that in a year?

options.text: About ₹1,500
options.explanation: That's one month (₹50 × 30).

options.text: About ₹18,000
options.explanation: ₹50 × 365 = ₹18,250. Small habits add up.

options.text: About ₹5,000
options.explanation: It's more than three times that.

options.text: Too little to matter
options.explanation: ₹18,000 could fund a course or an emergency fund.

title: Understand Investing quiz
description: Five questions on risk, time, compounding and diversification. Education only, never advice.

questions.prompt: Which statement about risk and return is true?

options.text: Options with higher possible returns usually have bigger ups and downs
options.explanation: Higher potential return is the reward for accepting more uncertainty.

options.text: High returns can be guaranteed if you pick carefully
options.explanation: No one can guarantee market returns.

options.text: Low-risk options always beat high-risk ones
options.explanation: Over long periods riskier assets have often grown more, but with no guarantee.

options.text: Risk only matters for large amounts
options.explanation: Risk applies to every rupee invested.

questions.prompt: Asha starts saving ₹500 a month at 18; Kiran starts at 28 with the same amount and rate. At 40, who likely has more?

options.text: Asha, because her money compounds for 10 extra years
options.explanation: Starting early gives compounding more time.

options.text: Kiran, because he is older and wiser
options.explanation: Age doesn't change the maths; time invested does.

options.text: Both the same
options.explanation: Asha deposits more AND her money grows longer.

options.text: It depends only on luck
options.explanation: Time and regular saving matter a lot.

questions.prompt: Zippy Gadgets falls 45% after a product failure. Whose fictional portfolio is hurt least?

options.text: Someone with 100% in Zippy Gadgets
options.explanation: They lose 45% of everything.

options.text: Someone with 10% in Zippy and the rest in a broad basket and deposit
options.explanation: Only a small slice is affected: the point of diversification.

options.text: Someone with 50% Zippy, 50% Sunrise Solar
options.explanation: Two single companies still means high concentration.

options.text: Everyone loses the same
options.explanation: The loss depends on how much was in Zippy.

questions.prompt: Markets fall 25% this year. Which investor is in the best position to wait for a possible recovery?

options.text: A student who needs the money for fees next month
options.explanation: She may have to sell at a loss.

options.text: Someone investing for a goal 15 years away
options.explanation: A long horizon gives time to wait, though recovery is never guaranteed.

options.text: Someone who borrowed money to invest
options.explanation: Debt repayments may force selling at a loss.

options.text: All are equally placed
options.explanation: Timeline is what decides whether you can wait.

questions.prompt: A simulation shows your fictional ₹10,000 could end between ₹7,000 and ₹19,000 in 5 years. What does this range mean?

options.text: You will definitely get ₹19,000
options.explanation: Simulations show possibilities, not promises.

options.text: Outcomes are uncertain; a loss is possible even though growth is likely
options.explanation: Ranges communicate uncertainty honestly.

options.text: The average of ₹13,000 is guaranteed
options.explanation: Even averages are assumptions.

options.text: The simulation is broken because it doesn't give one answer
options.explanation: Real investing has no single known answer.

title: Stay Financially Safe quiz
description: Five questions on OTPs, phishing, too-good offers and protecting your data.

questions.prompt: To RECEIVE ₹500 from a friend on UPI, you need to:

options.text: Enter your UPI PIN
options.explanation: A PIN only sends money. Never enter it to receive.

options.text: Share your UPI ID or let them scan your QR; no PIN needed
options.explanation: Receiving needs no PIN or scanning from your side.

options.text: Scan the QR code they send you
options.explanation: Scanning someone's QR is for paying them.

options.text: Share your OTP with them
options.explanation: Never share OTPs with anyone.

questions.prompt: Which web address is most likely the genuine site of 'Deccan Bank'?

options.text: deccanbank-rewards.xyz
options.explanation: Extra words and odd endings are common in fakes.

options.text: deccan-bank-kyc.co
options.explanation: Look-alike domain with 'kyc' bait.

options.text: The address printed in the bank's official app or passbook
options.explanation: Get the address from a trusted source, not a message.

options.text: Any site with the bank's logo
options.explanation: Logos are easy to copy.

questions.prompt: You 'won' a lucky draw you never entered and must pay a ₹2,000 'tax' to claim. You should:

options.text: Pay, because tax on prizes is real
options.explanation: Genuine prize taxes aren't collected by strangers via UPI.

options.text: Ignore, block and report it
options.explanation: A prize you never entered plus a fee = scam.

options.text: Send half and ask for proof
options.explanation: Any payment is lost money.

options.text: Share your bank details so they can deposit the prize
options.explanation: Never share details with unknown senders.

questions.prompt: A loan app wants access to your contacts and photo gallery before giving a loan. This is a warning sign because:

options.text: Illegal lenders use contacts and photos to harass and blackmail borrowers
options.explanation: Regulated lenders don't need your gallery or contacts.

options.text: It's normal for all loans
options.explanation: Over-broad permissions are not normal for lending.

options.text: It's fine if the app has good ratings
options.explanation: Ratings can be faked.

options.text: Only a problem if you don't repay
options.explanation: Your data can be misused regardless.

questions.prompt: A classmate asks you to send a photo of your Aadhaar so they can 'register you' for a free coaching offer. What's best?

options.text: Send it; they're a classmate
options.explanation: Even friends' phones can be compromised, and the offer itself may be a data scam.

options.text: Check the offer through the coaching centre's official site or a teacher, and register yourself if it's real
options.explanation: Verify the source and share documents only with the verified organisation.

options.text: Send a masked copy to everyone who asks
options.explanation: Masking helps, but sharing with unverified people is still risky.

options.text: Post it in the class group so everyone can register together
options.explanation: Never post ID documents in groups.

title: Final check
description: 12 questions covering the same ideas as your starting check, with new situations. Compare where you started with where you are now.

questions.prompt: Farhan has ₹800 left for the month. Which should he pay for first?

options.text: Printouts for a project due tomorrow
options.explanation: An essential study expense with a deadline.

options.text: A trending T-shirt
options.explanation: A want that can wait.

options.text: A gaming top-up on sale
options.explanation: Sales create urgency, not need.

options.text: Split equally across all three
options.explanation: Needs should be fully covered first.

questions.prompt: Divya earns ₹6,000 and her needs cost ₹4,500. Which budget is healthiest?

options.text: Needs ₹4,500, savings ₹900, wants ₹600
options.explanation: Balanced, with savings set aside first.

options.text: Needs ₹4,500, wants ₹1,500, savings ₹0
options.explanation: No savings leaves her exposed to surprises.

options.text: Needs ₹3,500, wants ₹2,500
options.explanation: Underfunding needs to buy wants backfires.

options.text: Needs ₹4,500, wants ₹2,000
options.explanation: That's ₹6,500, more than she has.

questions.prompt: A ₹2,000 course starts in 4 months. What monthly saving reaches the goal?

options.text: Save whatever is left each month
options.explanation: No target means no guarantee.

options.text: ₹2,000 in the final month
options.explanation: Last-minute saving rarely works.

questions.prompt: Which plan builds savings most reliably?

options.text: Automatically moving ₹200 to savings on payday
options.explanation: Automatic, first-thing saving removes temptation.

options.text: Saving only when there's a festival bonus
options.explanation: Irregular saving grows slowly.

options.text: Saving leftover coins at month end
options.explanation: Leftovers are small and unreliable.

options.text: Waiting until income is higher
options.explanation: The habit matters more than the amount.

questions.prompt: Your bicycle breaks and repair costs ₹600. You have a ₹1,000 emergency fund and ₹1,500 saved for a course. What's best?

options.text: Pay from the emergency fund and rebuild it over the next months
options.explanation: That's what it's for; your course savings stay intact.

options.text: Pay from course savings and keep the emergency fund untouched
options.explanation: This sets back your goal while the fund sits unused.

options.text: Borrow ₹600 from a moneylender
options.explanation: Borrowing when you have a cushion adds cost and risk.

options.text: Leave it broken and walk
options.explanation: If it's essential transport, delays cost you more.

questions.prompt: ₹2,000 at 10% compound interest yearly. Balance after 2 years?

options.explanation: That's simple interest (₹200 + ₹200).
Compounding doesn't double money that fast at 10%.
That's only after year 1.

questions.prompt: A friend's 'scheme' promises to double your money in 3 months, no risk. What do you conclude?

options.text: Unrealistic, guaranteed returns: very likely a fraud or Ponzi scheme
options.explanation: High return with no risk does not exist.

options.text: Safe because a friend recommended it
options.explanation: Friends can be fooled too; many schemes spread through friends.

options.text: Try with a small amount first
options.explanation: Early payouts are bait for bigger deposits.

options.text: Risk doesn't apply to short schemes
options.explanation: Promised high returns always carry risk.

questions.prompt: Which fictional portfolio is least likely to be wiped out by one company's failure?

options.text: 100% in Sunrise Solar
options.explanation: Everything rides on one company.

options.text: 50% Growth Basket, 30% Balanced Basket, 20% Steady Deposit
options.explanation: Spread across many companies and a deposit.

options.text: 50% Zippy Gadgets, 50% another gadget company
options.explanation: Same industry, same risks.

options.text: Whatever rose most last week
options.explanation: Chasing recent winners concentrates risk.

questions.prompt: You need ₹15,000 for a laptop in 6 months. How much market risk is appropriate for that money?

options.text: Very little; keep it steady because the deadline is close
options.explanation: A short horizon leaves no time to recover from a fall.

options.text: Lots; higher risk means faster growth
options.explanation: Higher risk can also mean a loss right when you need the money.

options.text: Put it all in one trending company
options.explanation: Concentrated and short-term: double risk.

options.text: Timeline doesn't matter
options.explanation: It is one of the most important factors.

questions.prompt: A 'delivery agent' calls asking for the OTP you received to 'confirm your parcel'. You should:

options.text: Refuse; never share an OTP you didn't request for your own use
options.explanation: The OTP may be authorising a payment or account access.

options.text: Share it because you're expecting a parcel
options.explanation: Scammers time calls to seem believable.

options.text: Share half of it
options.explanation: Never share any part.

options.text: Share it if the caller knows your name
options.explanation: Names are easy to find.

questions.prompt: An email styled like your scholarship portal says your payment failed: 'Click here within 2 hours to re-verify bank details.' Best response?

options.text: Click quickly before the deadline
options.explanation: The deadline is designed to rush you.

options.text: Open the official portal yourself (not via the link) and check your status
options.explanation: Go directly to the source you already know.

options.text: Reply with your bank details
options.explanation: Never send bank details in reply to messages.

options.text: Forward it to classmates to warn them, then click it
options.explanation: Don't click suspicious links at all.

questions.prompt: A website offers a ₹70,000 phone for ₹4,999 if you pay right now through UPI. This is most likely:

options.text: A rare genuine deal
options.explanation: Discounts that large are bait.

options.text: A scam: unrealistic price plus pressure to pay immediately
options.explanation: Too good to be true + urgency = classic scam.

options.text: Safe if the site looks professional
options.explanation: Professional-looking sites are easy to build.

options.text: Fine if you pay only half now
options.explanation: Any payment to a scam is lost.
